title: Weaponising NAPLAN: How Underachievement Is Being Used to Indict Explicit Instruction
author: The Disruptive Educator
summary: The Disruptive Educator takes down a wave of social-media criticism arguing that Australia's 2026 NAPLAN results disprove explicit instruction. The author's central move is a timeline check: Victoria's explicit-teaching model (VTLM 2.0) has been in implementation for barely a year, and New South Wales's push for under two, meaning no national test could plausibly show system-wide effects yet, especially since the current Year 9 cohort spent 6-7 years in school before either reform began. The piece also flags the logical inconsistency of critics who credit explicit instruction for a numeracy gain while blaming it for a literacy decline in the same breath, and argues that persistent underachievement — captured starkly in Pamela Snow's statistic that 132,857 of 1.3 million tested students are not keeping pace — is the reason schools adopted evidence-based literacy programs, not evidence that those programs failed. Case studies of Djidi Djidi Aboriginal School and Marsden Road Public School are used to show what turnaround under explicit instruction actually looks like once given more than a year to run. The essay closes by reframing the socioeconomic-gap data (disadvantaged Year 3 students already a year behind, five years behind by Year 9) as the real story critics are missing while chasing a policy-scoring narrative.
points: The core rebuttal is a timeline argument: Victoria's VTLM 2.0 (2025) and NSW's explicit-teaching mandate (mid-2024) haven't been running long enough for any current Year 3, 5, 7, or 9 cohort to have experienced them for a full schooling career, so 2026 NAPLAN results can't yet test their system-wide impact.

Pamela Snow's statistic — 132,857 of 1.3 million tested students not keeping up with basic classroom learning — is used to reframe the debate: persistent underachievement predates and motivated the shift to explicit instruction, rather than resulting from it.

The author catches critics in a causal double standard: crediting 'evidence' (i.e., explicit instruction) for numeracy gains is dismissed as overreach, while the same critics blame explicit instruction for literacy declines in the identical dataset.

Case studies of Djidi Djidi Aboriginal School and Marsden Road Public School — both moving from severe underachievement to above-average progress after adopting explicit instruction — are offered as concrete counter-evidence to the 'it isn't working' narrative.

Anna Stokke's line that 'all you can tell from a standardised test is a kid's postal code' anchors the piece's real argument: socioeconomic disadvantage, not instructional method, is the variable most responsible for the achievement gaps NAPLAN reveals.
quotes: The short story on NAPLAN is that it shows a persisting pattern of under-achievement in literacy and numeracy by about a third of Australian students.
To put this into real terms 132,857 of the 1.3 million children in Years 3, 5, 7 and 9 not keeping up with basic classroom learning.

In schools across the country that have used explicit teaching methods for a while, what's sometimes called phonics, and small group tutoring, where you give kids who are struggling extra intensive help, we are seeing big leaps.
In plain terms, the 2026 NAPLAN results cannot possibly tell us anything about the impact of statewide pushes for explicit instruction. Takes a little longer than that to turn a ship one would think.
Four years ago, testing at Djidi Djidi Aboriginal School revealed 16 of the 18 students in years 5 and 6 were at or below year 3 level in literacy.
If we were sending 100 kids to high school, 90 of them couldn't read or write as per their age — and that's failing those students.
All you can tell from a standardised test is a kid's postal code
More advantaged students will tend to be academically successful despite the choices we make, whereas the performance of less advantaged students is more likely to be because of what we've done
